articles.title: Cotton prices surge ₹4,000 a candy, T.N. textile mills fret over costs
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Cotton prices have surged ₹4,000 a candy in the past 10 days, barely 22 days into the 2026-27 cotton marketing season, raising concerns among more than 1,500 textile mills in Tamil Nadu over rising input costs.
“Cotton arrivals are not as expected for a couple of reasons,” said Nishant Asher, secretary of the Indian Cotton Federation.

Cotton prices have risen from ₹64,000 to ₹68,000 a candy on an ex-gin basis, an unusual increase for October. The anticipated decline in production, farmers holding back stocks in expectation of higher prices, and the scheduled reimposition of import duty from November 1 are contributing to the price rise, Mr. Asher said.

According to Durai Palaniswamy, chairman of the Southern India Mills’ Association, domestic cotton consumption in the 2025-26 season, which ended on September 30, 2026, stood at 336 lakh bales. Despite imports of 67 lakh bales, closing stocks were just 40 lakh bales.7

“Cotton farmers will not lose this year as the production is expected to be just 260 lakh bales as against a demand of 360 lakh bales. This is going to keep prices strong. However, if the import duty is reimposed, the textile industry will lose its competitiveness,” he said, calling for a balanced approach that will benefit the industry and the farmers.

articles.title: What is PHP and why is it facing a security crisis | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Story so far: On October 21, 2026, the team behind PHP announced two serious security flaws. In simple terms, a hacker could use them to break into a website’s server from far away, without needing physical access or a password. Security experts around the world have warned that the flaws could let attackers take control of affected servers.
PHP is a programming language that runs behind the scenes on websites. You never see it, but you use it all the time.

Say you log into your bank’s website or book a movie ticket. Your details travel to a server, which checks who you are, looks up your information and sends back the right page. PHP is often the tool doing that work.

It’s especially common in the systems that power online shops, blogs, news sites, membership sites and business tools. If something goes wrong with PHP, a lot of websites can be affected at once. That’s true whether it’s a small shop on cheap shared hosting or a big company with hundreds of servers.

Think of a computer’s memory as a huge set of shelves. Programs put things on the shelves, take them off and tidy up when they’re done. Good software has to keep careful track of what’s where, especially when something goes wrong halfway through a task.
The two flaws are both mistakes in this tidying-up process.

The first is a problem with running out of space. When PHP runs low on memory, it can end up handling half-finished data badly while cleaning up. This can leave the shelves in a mess, which is called “memory corruption.”

The second is a stale note. In some error situations, PHP keeps a note pointing to a shelf that has already been cleared. Later, it tries to use what it thinks is there, but finds something else entirely.

A skilled attacker can sometimes use these messes to sneak in their own instructions and make the server run them. That’s called “remote code execution.” If PHP has enough permissions on the server, an attacker could read private data, steal passwords or change what your website shows.

There’s another catch. These flaws sit deep inside PHP itself, so they can be triggered before a website’s own protections, such as login checks, get a chance to step in. A website can have strong security of its own and still be exposed.

According to the PHP Foundation, the group that supports PHP, the first flaw was spotted in 2024 during a security review. It took a long time to sort out, and the Foundation has admitted there were delays. Both flaws were made public this month, along with fixes.

That doesn’t mean hackers have been using them for two years. Finding a flaw, working out whether it can really be abused, reporting it safely and proving someone actually attacked are all separate steps.

articles.title: Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

articles.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

articles.title: Economics beyond the individual
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford’s work modelling the macroeconomy based on individual agents’ decisions has significant implications for monetary policy. Despite being hailed as providing a rigorous foundation for stabilisation policies, focusing on the individual blinds us to the way the macroeconomy actually works. It may seem paradoxical; John Maynard Keynes’s insight was that the aggregate economy cannot be understood simply as the sum of individual actions. Heterodox economics, by focusing on the structure of the broader economy rather than its individual components, provides a much better framework for understanding the economy.
The work of Keynes in the wake of the Great Depression led to the development of the study of the aggregate economy, as opposed to studying demand and supply of individual commodities.
Microeconomics focuses on the optimising behaviour of the individual, while macroeconomics focuses on statistical relationships to characterise aggregate behaviour.

Hall and Woodford provided rigorous models that rooted the study of macroeconomic aggregates, such as consumption, investment and employment, in the behaviour of individual agents. A key contribution was linking consumption to interest rates and the future. Individuals chose to smooth consumption over their lifetimes rather than base it solely on their current needs.

When interest rates were high, savings yielded greater returns. Individuals therefore had an incentive to defer some consumption to earn more and consume more in the future. Higher interest rates could reduce current consumption and hence lower current demand, and vice versa. Macroeconomic dynamics could consequently be derived from rigorous formulations of how individuals responded to market signals and policy variables such as interest rates.

This provided a framework within which Central Bankers could target an interest rate that was ‘neutral’ to the real economy — one that neither excessively stimulated nor depressed aggregate demand — greatly aiding the development of sophisticated stabilisation paradigms for monetary policy.

However, this approach collapsed the distinction between consumption, savings and investment. By viewing consumption inter-temporally, and by making it the main component of demand, the microfoundations methodology relegated the importance of volatile investment expectations to the background. Whatever was not consumed currently was saved, and automatically translated into future consumption demand. This was the framework followed by classical economics, which Keynes contested. He cautioned that not all saving is necessarily undertaken for future consumption.

In contrast, investment is fuelled by expectations of business owners as to prospects of profit. There is no necessity for the savings behaviour of individuals to always imply a demand for future consumption, and hence investment, by businesses. How can businesses determine whether an act of individual savings is to spend on a house for the future, or to ward against a future health emergency that may or may not occur? In such a situation, the interest rate cannot serve as an indicator of the extent of future consumption.
Keynes further suggested a radical intervention. It was not the interest rate that equated savings and investment, but income. Investment raised income, and generated an equal amount of savings.

This is not merely a technical insight, but an important way in which to view policy. It is not savings or inter-temporal consumption demand that affects output growth and employment, but business investment. To understand why economies are prone to instability, one must examine the investment behaviour of companies rather than the consumption demands of individuals.

According to Keynes, investment being done for profit in an environment of uncertainty is the chief source of economic instability. In uncertain situations, it is rational for investors to follow the herd, investing during a boom for fear of missing out on speculative returns, and withdrawing investment in a recession for fear of loss. This is the reason why booms and recessions get amplified. The work of Keynesians such as Hyman Minsky and Jan Kregel offers great insight into how the financial behaviour of firms brought about the boom in housing construction and finance, as well as the recession in 2008. Much of the current stock market gains in the U.S. economy are being driven by AI hyperscalers, giving rise to concerns of a new bubble that might eventually burst. Such outcomes can be clearly discerned when viewed from a Keynesian lens.

Some might argue that it does not matter how one views the economy, if the framework designed to bring about stability is effective. Moreover, in centering the actions of individuals, so the argument goes, this framework takes into account the reality of a complex economy being driven by individual choices.

articles.title: Why managing fiscal is a tightrope for State governments
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Kerala and Tamil Nadu are among the most socially and economically advanced States in India. Yet, the finances of both governments, like those of most other States, are under stress. The White Papers recently released by the two governments described their outstanding debt as alarming. State government debt is often vilified as the result of fiscal mismanagement. But it may, in fact, reflect a mismatch between development aspirations and the limited fiscal capacity of State governments.

Debts build up over the years with deficits, which arise when the government’s expenditure overshoots its tax and other receipts. In India, while the power to raise taxes rests largely with the Union government, a larger share of overall government spending is borne by the State governments. A majority of the State government expenditure is on social sectors, such as health and education, and economic sectors, such as agriculture and irrigation, all of which have a direct impact on people’s lives and livelihoods. In Kerala, the high levels of State government spending on social sectors since the 1960s have been a central constituent of the public action driving social progress. Compared with the corresponding average for all Indian States, per capita State government social expenditure was higher in Kerala and Tamil Nadu (by 30% and 20%, respectively). In contrast, it was markedly lower in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh (by 35% and 40%) (for the period 2020-23, according to an analysis based on State Finances: A Study of Budgets, Reserve Bank of India).

Central banks, through their toolkit of monetary policy, manage inflation, preserve confidence in the currency, and safeguard financial stability. articles.title: The reality behind falling net FDI
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: I ndia’s net foreign direct investment (FDI) has declined drastically in recent years. Critics see the weak net flows as a sign of weakness, while the Chief Economic Adviser points to the large inflows and rising manufacturing FDI as evidence of strength. He links weak net flows to profit repatriation and outward investment by Indian companies.

However, this debate overlooks a major issue. By focusing on overall numbers, both sides ignore the changing composition of international capital and the Balance of Payments (BoP) mechanisms that govern inflows and outflows.

For BoP purposes, net FDI is calculated as the difference between inflows and outflows after adjusting for the repatriation of capital. From the peak of $44.0 billion in 2020-21, net FDI fell to less than $1 billion in 2024-25. It recovered to $7.6 billion in 2025-26. The corresponding gross inflow was $94.6 billion.

It is necessary to note that India’s liberal FDI policy, introduced in 1991, initially emphasised technology acquisition, export promotion, and foreign exchange conservation. Over time, policy increasingly prioritised attracting larger inflows, while concerns regarding future external payment obligations and investment quality receded.

FDI is often viewed as a uniform, long-term commitment that brings technology and management skills to the host country. FDI can fall into three different investor classes, each with distinct capabilities, strategies, and exit timelines.

The first category is real FDI (RFDI), consisting of traditional multinational enterprises with the technology, brands, and capabilities to establish production and services. These generally represent long-term commitments.

The second category comprises financial investors, including private equity funds, venture capital firms, sovereign wealth funds, and asset managers. Their main goal is capital growth and planned exits.

The third category includes diaspora investments and special purpose vehicles (SPVs). These involve capital raised abroad and funneled through offshore financial centres, sometimes including the round-tripping of Indian funds.

Data on remittance-level FDI from the past four years, from 2022-23 to 2025-26 up to December, show that RFDI made up 41.9% of “effective inflows.” Financial investors followed closely with a 40.5% share, while the remaining 17.6% came from the diaspora and SPVs linked to India.

The business model of financial investors suggests future exits that result in large-scale capital repatriations. A notable example occurred in 2025 when Singapore’s Temasek exited Schneider Electric India Ltd., earning $6.4 billion on an investment of $637 million made in 2020. Total recorded divestment in CY 2025 was $52 billion, with 45 major foreign private equity and venture capital exits accounting for $29 billion in outflows.

Based on an analysis of effective inflows, FDI in India’s manufacturing sector has declined across three consecutive four-year periods. Most notably, RFDI into manufacturing accounted for only 10.6% of total effective inflows during the most recent four-year period.

A major blind spot in gross FDI figures is the mixing of new capital injections with corporate accounting changes, such as intra-group ownership reorganisations, mergers, share swaps, and the conversion of earlier non-equity instruments such as external commercial borrowings (ECBs) and convertible debentures.

articles.title: SBI’s cyber defences: What the bank had in place
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The suspected customer-data exposure at State Bank of India (SBI) has brought its cybersecurity preparedness into focus, despite the bank reporting an extensive array of safeguards in its annual disclosures.

SBI’s FY2025–26 Sustainability Report and Annual Report, published before the reported exposure, detail its security audits, automated threat monitoring, incident-response procedures and employee training. The disclosures also outline plans to further integrate its cyber-defence operations.

SBI’s Sustainability Report says information-systems audits covered 427 IT systems during FY26. Audits of outsourced IT activities covered 695 activities, while internal and external cybersecurity audits covered 176 IT applications and infrastructure and 151 systems, respectively.
However, the report does not disclose the findings, the number of vulnerabilities identified or how many were rectified. SBI reported “nil” instances of data breaches during FY26.

The bank’s Global Cyber Security Operations Centre (GCSOC) continuously monitors critical information systems for threats and unauthorised access. Automated tracking of indicators of compromise (IoCs)—digital clues that may signal cyberattacks—has replaced a previously manual process.
SBI also monitors phishing, fraudulent websites, brand impersonation, vishing and rogue mobile applications, pursuing the removal of malicious links and websites.

Its Annual Report cites an automated Secure Configuration Monitoring System covering more than 85,000 IT assets. AI-driven intelligence platforms, risk profiling and continuous monitoring of digital transactions help identify suspicious activity.

Security testing includes ethical hacking, vulnerability assessments, penetration testing and red-team exercises across websites, mobile applications, databases, networks and internal systems. Monthly domain-password-spray tests seek to identify employees using easily guessed passwords.
Firewalls, encryption, multi-factor authentication and data-loss prevention tools provide additional safeguards.

CERT SBI serves as the central first responder to cyber incidents. Its response framework covers detection, containment, eradication, recovery and post-incident reviews. A separate Incident Response Wing handles forensic investigations, threat hunting, mock drills and regulatory reporting.

SBI conducted 2,079 information-security and cybersecurity training programmes, benefiting 39,961 employees in FY26. Nearly 1.81 lakh employees had completed mandatory cybersecurity e-learning and assessments by March 31, 2026.
Oversight rests with the Board-level IT Strategy Committee, while the Group Chief Information Security Officer heads the Information Security Department.

articles.title: The broken promise of the right to work
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: On August 21, a three-judge Supreme Court Bench led by the Chief Justice of India dismissed a petition and sought a fresh one in a case on minimum wages in rural employment guarantee programmes. The Bench lauded MGNREGA’s role in rural development. It probed whether the ‘Right to Work’ should be treated on par with Article 21, the fundamental right to life, sparking an important discussion on the constitutional foundations of this right.

Despite its limited scope of only 100 days of work per rural household and chronic underfunding, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) was the only law anchored in the core principle of the right to work. In December 2025, the Union government replaced MGNREGA with the Viksit Bharat — Guarantee for Rozgar & Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-GRAM G) Act, and its implementation began on July 1. About 3.44 crore households worked for about 44 crore person-days under MGNREGA in July and August, on average, over the previous five years (Table 1) . There has been a 68% decrease in employment in July and August this year compared with the average of the preceding five years. Notwithstanding the proverbial ‘teething issues’, the dismantling of MGNREGA’s demand-driven right-to-work framework and the disproportionate fiscal burden that the new law places on States are likely to be major factors behind the dramatic fall in employment under the VB-GRAM G Act.

The impact of taking away even this limited right to work is therefore palpable. Discussions around the recent Supreme Court observations on the right to work can be traced back to the Constituent Assembly debates.

While most members agreed that a right to work was vital, the debate rested on whether it should be a fundamental right or be part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). The DPSPs do not automatically constitute rights but are meant to serve as precepts for governments to formulate laws and policies. This became the basis of the differences in perspective.

Professor K.T. Shah had strongly advocated recognising the right to work as a fundamental right, arguing that the State needed a constitutional and positive legal mandate to guarantee socio-economic security to its citizens. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, among others, held that while the right to work was an essential goal, its immediate universal enforcement was not fiscally and institutionally viable in a newly independent India that had been hollowed out of its resources. The placement of the right within the Directive Principles, rather than among the fundamental rights, thus reflected a deliberate constitutionalism of aspiration, rather than an abandonment of the welfare ideal. As scholars Anjani Kapoor and Manu Bhagwan have written in their essay ‘Ambedkar and the anti-isolation of Fellowship’, “The constitution does not establish the nation, but rather provides the tools to help achieve it.”

Therefore, Article 41 of the DPSP states: ‘The State shall, within the limits of its economic capacity and development, make effective provision for securing the right to work…” Embodying stronger progressive consecrations, Articles 39, 42 and 43 call for the “right to an adequate means of livelihood, equal pay for equal work for both men and women, just and humane conditions of work” and to “secure to all workers a living wage and decent standard of life.”

The Supreme Court, in Olga Tellis vs Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), ruled that the right to livelihood was a necessary condition for the fundamental right to life, giving a judicial fillip to the right to work. Spurred by the collective efforts of activists and rural workers, the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was passed in 2005. Although limited in scope, it made a pan-India right-to-work law a reality for the first time. The State had to ensure its statutory obligation to provide employment at minimum wages.

In 2009, MGNREGA wages were delinked from the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. Over time, MGNREGA wages barely kept pace with inflation and continued to remain lower than the minimum agricultural wages in most States. Low wages and an inadequate budget for generating employment have resulted in a steep decline in household earnings, with estimated total household earnings halving in July and August this year compared with the same months last year (Figure 1) .

During the recent hearing, the Supreme Court Bench remarked that if financial resources remained the same, having a minimum wage threshold could reduce the number of workers who could be provided employment. This remark, which appears to align with the Union government’s approach to employment guarantee, merits scrutiny on at least two counts.

First, it vitiates the judgment in Sanjit Roy vs State of Rajasthan (1983) where the Supreme Court observed that payment of wages below minimum wages violates Article 23 of the Constitution and is akin to ‘forced labour.’ Second, it rests on a misleading economic logic that financial resources to implement a welfare programme must remain unchanged and constrained.

In reality, higher wages for rural workers increase their purchasing power, enhance their freedoms, and improve human development outcomes. These, in turn, increase effective demand for goods and services, creating a positive multiplier effect, resulting in higher economic productivity. Therefore, higher government spending on an employment guarantee programme at increased wages can yield a mutually reinforcing cycle between development and growth.

By putting an arbitrary cap on funds for the VB-GRAM G Act and not linking it with minimum wages, the very notion of employment guarantee stands delegitimised. States are already grappling with fiscal constraints and curtailed borrowing limits under the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) framework. The increased burden of funding the VB-GRAM G Act will prevent States from generating employment. The sharp drop in employment and earnings is a reflection of this change.

articles.title: Agrivoltaics on 10% of suitable land can meet 2050 power demand: Pralhad Joshi
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Operationalising just 10% of the agricultural land deemed suitable for agrivoltaics in India could generate enough electricity to meet the country’s projected power demand for 2050, Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi said on Tuesday.

“If even 10% [of the land deemed suitable for agrivoltaics] is converted [towards operationalisation], more than whatever power requirement is being estimated for 2050 can be generated by agrivoltaics,” he said, citing a study by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI).
Published in July, the study identified about 47.5 million hectares, or nearly 30% of India’s more than 160 million hectares of arable agricultural land, as suitable for agrivoltaics.

The approach combines agricultural activity with solar photovoltaic power generation on the same land, potentially allowing farmers to retain agricultural production while earning additional income from renewable energy.

The government is working on a dedicated policy framework for the sector, with agrivoltaics potentially being incorporated into the next phase of the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan (PM-KUSUM).
“We will be launching one of the world’s agrivoltaic programmes under the next phase of PM Kusum,” Mr. Joshi said at the inauguration of the seventh Agrivoltaics World Conference.

Speaking at the conference, Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan highlighted the potential benefits of agrivoltaics but stressed the need to address land-use concerns and assess the feasibility of projects across different regions.

Mr. Joshi said agrivoltaic installations, which typically require elevated solar panel structures to facilitate farming underneath, could cost 25-30% more than conventional ground-mounted solar projects.
He stressed the need to bridge the cost differential to make the model commercially viable.

“The average cost of electricity supply was around ₹7 per unit in [fiscal year] 2025-26. While some of the major agrivoltaics assessment indicate potential generation of ₹3.20 to 3.30 [per unit], whereas ground mounted costs now ₹2.5 to 2.6 [per unit]. This difference has to be matched,” he said.

Mr. Chouhan said the proposed policy must provide mechanisms to help farmers repair solar modules, address disputes and clarify the terms under which agricultural land can be sold or leased, even as he hailed agrivoltaics’ potential for additional revenue generation.
“There must be participation [from farmers] but coinciding with mechanisms to facilitate resolutions as well,” he said.

articles.title: Rupee strengthens for eighth consecutive day on IPO inflows; rise in crude prices cap gains
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The rupee strengthened for the eighth consecutive session on Wednesday (October 21, 2026), buoyed by foreign fund inflows linked to the Jio Platforms IPO. However, a sharp rise in crude oil prices capped its gains amid concerns over imported inflation.

The rupee closed at 94.46 against the U.S. dollar, its strongest level in over a month, after touching an intraday high of 94.43. It pared some gains as benchmark Brent crude prices climbed to $110 a barrel.

The $3.2-billion Jio Platforms IPO, India’s largest initial public offering, opened for subscription on Wednesday (October 21) and was fully subscribed as foreign investors rushed to participate in the issue.

“Going forward, movements in the dollar index, crude oil prices and foreign portfolio flows will remain key drivers, with geopolitical uncertainty continuing to pose risks to the currency,” Anil Kumar Bhansali, head of treasury at Finrex Treasury Advisors LLP, said in a note.

In contrast to the rupee’s gains, the benchmark 10-year government securities (G-Sec) yield rose to 7.44% on Wednesday (October 21, 2026), its highest level since 2023, as surging crude prices intensified inflationary concerns. Bond prices and yields move inversely.

Uncertainty over a resolution to the ongoing West Asia crisis, coupled with concerns over imported inflation, continued to weigh on the bond market. India’s retail inflation rose to a higher-than-expected 5.54% in September, bringing it closer to the Reserve Bank of India’s upper tolerance limit of 6%.
Venkatkrishnan Srinivasan, founder and managing partner of Rockfort Fincap LLP, expects the benchmark 10-year yield to trade in the 7.25%-7.50% range.
“On a durable basis, if the crude remains above $100 for the next 25 days, yields could even rise as high as 7.60%,” he said.

articles.title: Anticipation over upcoming EU FTA more than doubles Ferrari orders in India
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Ferrari has seen more than a doubling of its orders from India in anticipation of the Free Trade Agreement (FTA) between India and the European Union that is set to come into force in early 2027, top officials of the luxury car company said. The FTA will see a substantial lowering of import tariffs on European cars entering the Indian market.

Speaking at a select media roundtable in New Delhi, Ferrari’s heads for Southeast Asia, and the Far and Middle East further said that, over the last two years, the company has restructured itself internally to forefront India in its global plans.

So many of the people are already walking to our dealership every day to say, ‘okay, I know the FTA is coming, can I start to configure my car, can I start to have an idea of the price, etc’,” Charles Antoine Geneste, Head of Southeast Asia at Ferrari said. “So, we can clearly see the passion that was there, and that there is this acceleration that for us is amazing to see.”

Since Ferrari typically likes to maintain a waiting period of 18 months between placing an order and delivery of a car, Mr. Geneste said that customers in India are already lining up to place orders so that they can get delivery once the FTA is in effect.

While declining to quantify exactly how much demand has increased in anticipation of the FTA, when asked if it has doubled, Ferrari’s President of Far and Middle East Francesco Bianchi said: “See, this is big, it’s more than what you say.”

Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to be in Brussels on December 16 for the signing of the India-EU FTA, and the European authorities say that it is expected to come into force in “early 2027” once the European Parliament has cleared it.

Under the deal, India has agreed to slash import duties on European-made luxury car Completely Built Units (CBUs) from around 110% to 30-35% in the first year, which will further drop to 10% in a phased manner, subject to initial annual quotas.

Ferrari has currently opened its experiential exhibition ‘Universo Ferrari’ in New Delhi up to November 1, where it showcases its key models, including the Formula One race car as well as its Le Mans model, apart from its various luxury streetcars.

This exhibition, so far launched in only five countries worldwide, including its home country of Italy, is the latest in a series of moves Ferrari has made over the last few years to increasingly cater to the India market.

“We deliberately decided to have a team that is focused on India and Southeast Asia,” Mr Bianchi said. “We found that the previous structure that we had was not effective enough to really expand the potential of a market like India.”

“We prefer to grant India maximum visibility,” he added. “So, basically the team that is also managing the Southeast Asia markets is now owning India and India is for sure the main engine of this region.”

articles.title: Fall of the centre: on the public discontent in France
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: When Emmanuel Macron came to power in 2017 , at age 39, he promised to keep extremist political forces at bay, build a new France through his ‘revolution’, rejuvenate economic growth, manage debt and create employment opportunities. Nine years later, with six months to go for France’s next presidential election, Mr. Macron, whose approval rating is at an abysmally low 15%, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu , who lacks a parliamentary majority, are struggling to restore order in a country battered by economic woes, street protests, violent riots and a surging far right. Even in France, where protests are part of the political culture, Saturday’s (October 17, 2026) riots and looting were a shock with at least 3,000 businesses and shops damaged. Municipal halls were attacked and buildings set on fire , including the 19 th -century Limoges town hall. Some 2,400 people were arrested and Prime Minister Lecornu called for local curfews . The trigger for the unrest was a move by Mr. Lecornu to pass budget proposals raising some taxes and freezing spending on social programmes. When school students hit the streets with demands for better educational facilities, the government responded with force and tear gas. But its heavy-handed response helped the student protest snowball into an anti-government movement, culminating in riots.

To understand the precarious situation France is in today, all one has to do is to look at the macroeconomic numbers. Growth remains sluggish with the economy estimated to expand by a mere 0.8% in 2026, while the unemployment rate stands at 8.3%. The core problem is the country’s public finances. France’s national debt stands at 120% of GDP, the third highest in the eurozone, after Greece and Italy. The French Treasury’s debt servicing bill is expected to reach about €60 billion in 2026. When Mr. Macron came to power, he reduced corporate taxes and sought to restrain public spending to stimulate growth. But growth remained sluggish while public debt ballooned. When protests gripped the country in 2018-19, he offered economic concessions, but with no long-term solutions to the structural problems the French economy was facing. In 2024, he called snap elections to blunt the far-right momentum. After the elections, he invited a leader from smaller blocs to form a government to keep the left-wing New Popular Front, the largest bloc, out of power, deepening the political crisis and weakening his position. This is Emmanuel Macron’s legacy. Worse, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right, anti-immigrant National Rally, could exploit the chaos and public anger to her benefit ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

articles.title: Unknown vulnerabilities: on the cybersecurity advisory by CERT-In
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The cybersecurity advisory by the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has outlined two threat vectors vis-à-vis Indian commercial and government IT infrastructure: AI companies testing autonomous agents exceeding their designated operational constraints and bad actors weaponising open-source agentic AI tools for automated reconnaissance and exploitation. However, the organisations affected by recent breaches that the advisory was based on did not detect them: they came to light in the AI companies’ disclosures and CERT-In operations. Aside from developers allowing experimental systems to act outside their authorised bounds, the advisory highlights two problems for India — existing arrangements focus on cybersecurity incidents after they are revealed; and the implicated organisations being found under-prepared for the DPDP Act — to be enforced from 2027, including steep penalties on entities not maintaining reasonable safeguards against breaches. While CERT-In observed or received reports of 29.4 lakh incidents in 2025, it does not routinely publish postmortem analyses and is exempt from the RTI Act. As a result, public accountability is also weak: CERT-In found that the AI agents and/or bad actors exploited vulnerabilities, including exposed passwords, that are known security problems separate from AI agents’ abilities.

AI companies and labs have made several disclosures this year of agents unexpectedly breaching real-world infrastructure worldwide during testing. For India, however, the legal boundaries specified by the IT Act 2000 leave open an accountability gap for autonomous agents without the backing of human intentions. A more specific lacuna is that while CERT-In requires an organisation to report an intrusion within six hours, many organisations remain incapable of, or unwilling to, discover it. The reporting deadline itself has not ensured detection. Overall, the national cybersecurity landscape is fragmented across a pastiche of enforceable requirements in some domains, advisory technical standards in others, and narrow AI-specific accountability in yet others. As human and autonomous threat actors become more sophisticated, India needs to leapfrog to a landscape with enforceable risk-based requirements for both testing and defending against autonomous agents; better spotting unauthorised access, especially in the public sector; and a legal safe-harbour for security research conducted in good faith, in line with CERT-In policy. CERT-In should also publish more information, anonymised where necessary, which includes remediation outcomes and whether the affected individuals were informed. Finally, the government should also review the exemption for CERT-In from the RTI Act as such a sweeping exemption is unnecessary for effective cyber-defence.
